MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

steps.title: What iLit is
steps.text: iLit is a case law library of immigration litigation decisions, built for the CBSA Hearings and Litigation Division. It is designed to give more analytical insight than a plain search can, so that litigators can do better research and improve outcomes. This short tour shows the main features. Press Next to move along, Back to go back, or Exit at any time. The mouse moves and clicks for you, and before each move to a new page the card tells you where you are going next. Everything shown is the live site; the one sample memo is fictional. Where something is still being built, the card says so.

steps.title: Search for a case
steps.text: Everything starts with one search box. You can type a case name like Vavilov, a citation like 2019 SCC 65, or words from the reasons. Each result shows the citation, court, date and judge and, where known, how the case ended and how many other decisions cite it. Searching in plain words works, but the matching is still being improved.
steps.say: First, a search for a case by name: Vavilov.
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open Research, where most work starts.

steps.title: Narrow it down with filters
steps.text: The filters on the left narrow any search and all combine. The tour ticked the Refugee protection group, added the tags cessation and Sri Lanka, chose Government won and pressed Search. Case types and tags are a work in progress. Next it opens Veerasingam v. Canada from this list.

steps.title: The reader
steps.text: This is the reader. It has three parts. The header across the top gives the title, court, outcome, citation, date decided and decision maker, with a link back to the search and a button to save the decision to the Workbench. The side panel on the left holds what iLit found in the decision. The reader itself, on the right, shows the decision as a clean document with numbered paragraphs.
steps.lead: Next, let's open Veerasingam v. Canada
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open this refugee cessation decision, which it uses for the rest of the tour.

steps.title: The side panel: About
steps.text: The About tab holds the title and citation, the recorded outcome, the decision maker, how many decisions cite this one and how many cases and statutes it cites, the case details, and the topics found in the text with how often each appears.

steps.title: The side panel: Authorities
steps.text: The Authorities tab lists every case and statute the decision cites, with how many times and at which paragraphs, so you can move through the decision by its citations.

steps.title: The side panel: Intelligence, the judge
steps.text: The Intelligence tab opens with a judge snapshot: who decided this case, their decisions in the library and how often each side succeeded. Judge names are still being cleaned up, so a count can look thin. The full version is the Judge profiles page, which we visit later.

steps.title: The side panel: Intelligence, citations
steps.text: The other half of the Intelligence tab is a citation snapshot: how many decisions have cited this one, and with what results. The full version is Citation Intelligence, which we also visit later.

steps.title: The decision itself
steps.text: The decision is formatted with its numbered paragraphs. iLit marks what it finds in the text: citations to other cases in gold, statutes and regulations in purple, and topic tags in green. The buttons above the text turn each colour on or off. Everything marked comes from fixed rules read against the decision, and nothing is added to the text itself.

steps.title: A citation, previewed
steps.text: Hovering the mouse over a gold citation that names a paragraph shows the text of that paragraph, taken from the cited decision in the library. You can check what a case is being used for without leaving the page. That is the hover card. The next card shows what a click does.

steps.title: A citation, opened
steps.text: A click opens the cited passage as a card under the paragraph, in full. The pin keeps a card open while you keep reading, so a passage can be checked against the reasons. Double-clicking a citation opens that decision in a new tab. Statutes work the same way.

steps.title: Explore the reader
steps.text: Your turn. Scroll through the decision, hover over citations, open and pin cards, and click through the side panel tabs. Clicks that would take you to another page are paused during this step, so you cannot lose your place. Click Next when you are done and we will move on to Intelligence and Statistics.

steps.title: Citation Intelligence
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open Citation Intelligence, the full version of the reader's citation snapshot.
steps.text: The tour searched for Vavilov, the Supreme Court's leading decision on judicial review, by typing its name and picking it from the list. The figures count the decisions in the library that cite it. Outcomes are read by rules and can be wrong, so check the decision itself.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open the full version of the reader's judge snapshot.
steps.text: The tour searched for Justice Brouwer by typing the name in the list and opening the profile. It shows the judge's decisions and how often each side succeeded. The list is still being cleaned up, so counts are a guide.

steps.title: FC Analytics
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open the last page in this section.
steps.text: FC Analytics covers Federal Court immigration files, including the many that never reach a published decision. It is built from the Court's own registry. Next, the page opens for you to explore.

steps.title: Explore FC Analytics
steps.text: Your turn. Change the years filed, click a bar or a year to drill in, and scroll down to timing, deadlines, refusals and the decision makers under review. Clicks that would take you to another page are paused during this step. Click Next when ready to move on to the Analyst workbench.

steps.title: The analyst workbench
steps.text: The workbench is still in development. Eventually each analyst will have a log in and a space of their own for files, a case list, saved decisions and notes. The case list is meant to flag when the Federal Court docket moves on an analyst's IMM files. The demonstration account has no password.
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open it.

steps.title: Live analysis
steps.text: Live analysis lets an analyst plug in any Word file, text PDF or pasted draft, such as a memorandum of argument or a decision. iLit reads it with the same rules it uses on every decision in the library, so citations and statutes are recognised and linked. The document is read in memory, never saved, and never sent to an AI model.
steps.leadText: Press Next and the tour will open it.

steps.title: A Word file, dropped in
steps.say: We will drop in a fabricated Word document to demonstrate the functionality.
steps.text: This is a fictional Memorandum of Argument from a refugee cessation judicial review, written for this demonstration. In practice it could be the memo filed by opposing counsel, or a draft an analyst is preparing.

steps.title: The memo, marked up
steps.say: Read document runs the same rules used on the library.
steps.text: iLit went through the memo line by line. The counts show the case citations and statute references it found. Each one is marked in the text, as in the reader, so it can be previewed, opened as a card and pinned. A citation to a case in the library, such as Baker, links to that decision.

steps.title: What is live, and what is not
steps.text: Live today: search, the reader, citation and judge pages, Federal Court analytics and Live analysis. The Workbench is still being built. Still being improved: plain-word search, case types and tags, and judge names. iLit is built around the Federal Court, the Federal Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court. It is a research aid, not legal advice. To finish, explore what is coming soon.
steps.lead: Let's go back to the home page and wrap up the tour.
steps.leadText: A short summary of what is live and what is still being built.
